transcript.text: Turn this article into a roughly 90-second podcast chat between two hosts. Use two clearly different English voices, one male and one female, friendly and curious rather than newsreader-ish. Explain what tiny urban forests are and discuss the article's main points without making up facts. No music. Please give me the finished audio, not just a script.

Before I spend any of your credits, here's a limit you should know about. My Magic Hour tools have no plain text-to-speech or podcast-voice tool. None of them takes a two-person script and returns an audio file with a male and a female voice. The only way I can make speech from a script is through a video model (ltx-2.5 on your free plan) that makes people talking on camera, with sound.

So the closest I can get to what you want:
• I make the chat as a series of short video clips, two hosts at a podcast desk (one man, one woman) saying the lines below, then join them into one ~90-second file. No music.
• What you get is an MP4 with the dialogue as its sound track, not an audio-only file. You can pull the audio out in any free tool.
• Caveats: the model picks the voices itself. I'll ask for a friendly, curious man and woman, but I can't choose exact voices or promise they'll sound the same from clip to clip. It may also mangle some words now and then.
• Cost: about 24 credits per second, so roughly 2,100–2,200 credits for 90 seconds. On a free plan that may be more than you have, and the account will refuse the job if so.

Here's the draft script (about 90 seconds, using only facts from the article):

HOST A (woman): So, tiny forests. What are they?
HOST B (man): They're dense little forests planted on empty city lots, some about the size of a tennis court. Cities across Europe and Asia are doing it.
A: And there's a method behind it?
B: Yes, it comes from the Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. You plant three to five native saplings per square metre, in enriched soil.
A: That's crowded!
B: On purpose. The trees compete for light, so they grow quickly. Supporters say a tiny forest can look after itself in about three years.
A: What do people say they get out of it?
B: Cooler streets, more insects and birds, and a place where schoolchildren can learn.
A: Sounds great. Is there a catch?
B: Critics say the evidence is still thin. Many projects are too young to measure, and with planting that dense, a lot of saplings can die.
A: Fair point. Is there anything everyone agrees on?
B: One thing. Urban ecologists say a tiny forest is no substitute for protecting the big trees we already have. Those store far more carbon.
A: So plant the tiny forests, but keep the big old trees.
B: Exactly.

How do you want to go ahead?
1. Make it as the talking-hosts video described above (~2,100+ credits, voices not guaranteed).
2. Keep only the script. You could record it yourselves or paste it into a dedicated two-voice TTS tool, which will give you better control over the voices.
Tell me too if you want any changes to the script.
